meta.title: Antipsychotics app: domain data
meta.note: Single source of the domain data used and shown by the app: drug, molecular, receptor, route, regional and model data with their descriptive texts. Values are rounded literature values for teaching; each sourced value has an entry in "sources" that cites "references". Presentation settings (colors of plots, layout, animation) stay in the code.

units.drugs.*.smiles: SMILES (used to draw the 2D structure, tools/build_structures.py)
units.drugs.*.pd.ki: Ki per receptor target (nM, human cloned receptors): from section 12.2 of the FDA label where stated, otherwise the ChEMBL median; null = no appreciable affinity reported (typically IC50 > 1 µM); "nd" = not determined (no human value found)
units.drugs.*.pd.ia: intrinsic activity relative to the endogenous agonist (0-1) where the drug is a (partial) agonist at that target; absent = antagonist or inverse agonist
units.drugs.*.pd.ec50: plasma concentration of the D2-active moiety giving 50% striatal D2 occupancy in PET studies (ng/mL); calibrates dose to occupancy; null for drugs without D2 binding (free concentration = unbound plasma concentration)
units.drugs.*.pk.highFirstPass: true if hepatic extraction is high enough that bioavailability changes with hepatic clearance
units.drugs.*.pk.pathways: fraction of clearance by each pathway (sums to 1): cyp1a2, cyp2d6, cyp3a4, cyp2c19, ugt, renal, other
units.drugs.*.pk.ref: therapeutic reference range of the plasma concentration (ng/mL, AGNP consensus where available)
units.drugs.*.pk.metabolites[].fm: fraction of the precursor cleared to this metabolite (0-1)
units.drugs.*.pk.metabolites[].from: "parent" or the key of the metabolite it is formed from
units.drugs.*.pk.metabolites[].d2: true if the metabolite binds D2 like the parent and counts toward the active moiety
units.drugs.*.pk.rt.*.ka: absorption rate constant by this route (1/h); 0 = bolus
units.drugs.*.pk.rt.lai.tAbs_d: apparent absorption half-life of the depot (days); flip-flop kinetics
units.drugs.*.pk.rt.lai.products: depot products of the drug (keyed by product); each has name, F, dose, tau, label and release; marketed: false hides a product in a region; rt.lai.product is the default
units.drugs.*.pk.rt.*.release: release phases of a dose: f fraction of the dose; lag_d delay before release (days); dur_d release window at a constant rate (days; 0 = at once); tAbs_d absorption half-life from the release site (days; absent = straight into plasma)
units.drugs.*.pk.rt.*.tau: usual dosing interval by this route (h)
units.model.dopamine.K_nM: effective dissociation constant of dopamine at D2 in vivo (nM)
units.model.dopamine.tonic_nM: tonic striatal dopamine used to calibrate drug concentrations to PET occupancy (nM)
units.model.thresholds: striatal D2 occupancy (fraction) at which antipsychotic response, prolactin elevation and extrapyramidal symptoms become likely (PET)
units.dopaminePathways.*.da: default synaptic dopamine concentration for the pathway (nM)
units.routes[].onsetMin: typical onset of the calming effect (min); used to order and scale the onset bars
units.regions.abundance: relative abundance per target and region: level 0-3 (absent or trace, low, moderate, high) and the subregions or cell populations concerned; level null = not characterized (pituitary gland: only D2 is modeled)
units.modifiers.*.m: multiplier of the clearance of each pathway
units.drugs.*.pk.metabolites[].mw: molecular weight of the metabolite (g/mol), for molar concentration units
units.dopaminePathways.*.geometry.mni: approximate course of the pathway in MNI152 coordinates (mm), right hemisphere (mirrored for the left): one polyline per branch, from the origin nucleus to the target. The VTA and substantia nigra origins are placed in the anterior midbrain of the brainstem model (y -24 mm), a few mm posterior to their anatomical position in the ventral diencephalon, which the model does not show; each line ends where it reaches the surface of its target structure (MNI152 2009c segmentation, smoothed as the model meshes)
units.dopaminePathways.*.geometry.endpoint: "pituitary": the last point lies outside the brain model and is drawn as a marker
units.validation: observed pharmacokinetic endpoints (ng/mL of the analyte, h, ratios) with the regimen simulated: drug, route, product, region (default us), dose, tau, steadyState, initiation, analyte (parent, moiety or a metabolite key); set: calibration (used to fit) or validation (independent)
units.drugs.*.pd.action: qualitative action per target where it differs from antagonism ("agonist", "antagonist"), for drugs without numeric intrinsic activity
units.drugs.*.pd.components: co-formulated compounds (e.g. trospium in xanomeline-trospium): Ki per target (nM), drawn as an extra layer of the affinity radar
units.drugs.*.pk.apparent: true if F = 1 stands for apparent oral parameters (V/F and CL/F) because absolute bioavailability is not known
units.drugs.*.pk.components: co-formulated compounds simulated alongside the parent with their own PK; strengths = [parent mg, component mg] per capsule strength
units.targets.*.agonism: effect and clinical text shown on the target card when the selected drug is an agonist there (pd.action)
units.regions.abundance.*.*.activation: main consequence of activating that receptor in that region (empty: none established)
units.regions.abundance.*.*.blockade: main consequence of blocking that receptor in that region (empty: none established)
units.targets.*.signaling: principal G-protein coupling and second-messenger pathway of the receptor
units.regions.abundance.*.*.pathway: how the receptor in that region relates to the dopaminergic pathways, and the resulting effect (only where applicable)
units.chemGroups: chemical groups in sort order (gallery and substances table) with the core substructures (SMARTS, tried in order) on which the 2D drawings of a group are aligned (tools/build_structures.py)
units.drugs.*.chemGroup: key of the chemical group in chemGroups
units.drugs.*.pd.fec50: functional EC50 at the receptor measured in the laboratory (nM), for targets where the drug acts as a (partial) agonist; ChEMBL median
units.drugs.*.pd.femax: maximal effect in the same functional assays, relative to the full agonist (fraction 0-1); ChEMBL median
units.drugs.*.pk.refAnalyte: analyte of the therapeutic reference range: parent (the drug itself) or moiety (parent plus D2-active metabolites)
units.drugs.*.pk.metabolites.*.d2Weight: D2 potency of an active metabolite relative to the parent (weight in the D2-active moiety; default 1)
units.model.validation: acceptance criteria of the validation table

d2.label: D2
d2.location: Dorsal and ventral striatum (very high), substantia nigra and VTA (autoreceptors), pituitary lactotrophs; low in cortex
d2.clinical: All licensed antipsychotics except pimavanserin and xanomeline-trospium act at D2. PET studies place the antipsychotic window at ≈ 65-78% striatal occupancy, with prolactin elevation above ≈ 72% and EPS above ≈ 78% (Kapur et al. 2000).
d2.signaling: G<sub>i/o</sub>-coupled: inhibits adenylyl cyclase and opens GIRK potassium channels

d3.label: D3
d3.effect: Motivation, reward and mood; proposed contribution to negative symptoms and cognition
d3.location: Ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens shell), islands of Calleja, hypothalamus; substantia nigra
d3.clinical: Cariprazine binds D3 with ~6-fold higher affinity than D2 and occupies it substantially at clinical doses; this is the rationale for its use in predominant negative symptoms.

ht1a.label: 5-HT1A
ht1a.effect: Partial agonism: anxiolysis, antidepressant effect, possible reduction of EPS and improvement of negative symptoms
ht1a.location: Raphe nuclei (somatodendritic autoreceptors), hippocampus, limbic and prefrontal cortex
ht1a.clinical: Partial agonism by aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, lurasidone, ziprasidone and clozapine increases prefrontal dopamine release; buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist anxiolytic.
ht1a.signaling: G<sub>i/o</sub>-coupled: inhibits adenylyl cyclase and hyperpolarizes neurons through GIRK channels

ht2a.label: 5-HT2A
ht2a.effect: Antagonism / inverse agonism: lower EPS liability, improved slow-wave sleep; antipsychotic in Parkinson disease psychosis (pimavanserin)
ht2a.location: Neocortex (layer V pyramidal neurons, very high), claustrum, ventral striatum; platelets
ht2a.clinical: A 5-HT2A/D2 affinity ratio favoring 5-HT2A (Meltzer index) distinguishes most second-generation agents. Serotonergic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin) are 5-HT2A agonists.
ht2a.signaling: G<sub>q/11</sub>-coupled: activates phospholipase C (IP<sub>3</sub>, intracellular Ca<sup>2+</sup>)

ht2c.label: 5-HT2C
ht2c.effect: Antagonism: increased appetite and weight gain, impaired glucose regulation; possible antidepressant effect
ht2c.location: Choroid plexus (very high), hypothalamus (arcuate POMC neurons), substantia nigra, limbic regions
ht2c.clinical: Hypothalamic 5-HT2C blockade (with H1) is implicated in the weight gain of olanzapine and clozapine; the HTR2C −759C/T promoter variant modifies this risk.

h1.label: H1
h1.effect: Antagonism: sedation, increased appetite and weight gain
h1.location: Hypothalamus, thalamus, cortex and limbic system (targets of tuberomammillary histamine neurons)
h1.clinical: High H1 affinity (clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, chlorpromazine) predicts sedation and weight gain; low-dose quetiapine is used off-label for sleep for this reason.

m1.label: M1
m1.effect: Antagonism: anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, tachycardia), cognitive impairment and delirium; fewer EPS
m1.location: Cortex, hippocampus and striatum (high); peripheral glands and smooth muscle (with M3)
m1.clinical: Intrinsic antimuscarinic activity of clozapine, olanzapine and low-potency phenothiazines lowers EPS but causes constipation (clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility can be fatal) and cognitive impairment, particularly in older adults.

agonism.effect: Agonism: with M4 agonism, thought to underlie the antipsychotic effect of xanomeline
agonism.clinical: Trospium in the same capsule antagonizes muscarinic receptors mainly in peripheral tissues. The most common adverse reactions on the label are nausea, dyspepsia, constipation, vomiting, hypertension, abdominal pain, diarrhea, tachycardia, dizziness and gastro-esophageal reflux.

a1.label: α1
a1.effect: Antagonism: orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, falls and reflex tachycardia; sedation; priapism (rare)
a1.location: Thalamus and cortex; vascular smooth muscle (blood pressure)
a1.clinical: α1 blockade requires slow titration of clozapine, quetiapine, iloperidone and risperidone, particularly in older adults, to limit orthostatic hypotension and falls.
a1.signaling: G<sub>q/11</sub>-coupled: activates phospholipase C; contracts vascular smooth muscle

otherTargets.label: 5-HT7
otherTargets.effect: Circadian rhythm, sleep and mood regulation
otherTargets.clinical: 5-HT7 antagonism is proposed to contribute to the antidepressant effect of lurasidone and of low-dose amisulpride.

otherTargets.label: M1/M4
otherTargets.effect: M4 autoreceptor activation on striatal cholinergic interneurons and midbrain inputs reduces striatal dopamine release
otherTargets.clinical: Xanomeline-trospium is the first licensed antipsychotic without D2 blockade: no EPS or prolactin elevation; trospium, a peripherally restricted antagonist, limits cholinergic adverse effects (nausea, vomiting).

otherTargets.label: NET
otherTargets.clinical: Norquetiapine NET inhibition and 5-HT1A partial agonism are thought to underlie the antidepressant efficacy of quetiapine XR in bipolar depression.

otherTargets.label: hERG (Kv11.1)
facts: IV haloperidol, thioridazine, pimozide, sertindole, ziprasidone
otherTargets.clinical: ECG monitoring is advised with high-dose or intravenous haloperidol and with QT-prolonging co-medication; aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine and lurasidone have little QTc effect.

mesolimbic.label: Mesolimbic
mesolimbic.role: Excess presynaptic dopamine synthesis/release (PET studies) is linked to positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech and behavior); D2 blockade here is thought to underlie the antipsychotic effect.

nigrostriatal.label: Nigrostriatal
nigrostriatal.role: Motor control; D2 blockade here causes parkinsonism, acute dystonia and akathisia, and with chronic exposure tardive dyskinesia. Extrapyramidal symptoms become likely above about 78 % striatal D2 occupancy.

tuberoinfundibular.label: Tuberoinfundibular
tuberoinfundibular.role: Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release; the pituitary lies outside the blood-brain barrier, so poorly brain-penetrant drugs (amisulpride, risperidone, paliperidone) raise prolactin most.

geometry.targets: Median eminence and anterior pituitary (outside the blood-brain barrier)

mesocortical.label: Mesocortical
mesocortical.role: Low prefrontal dopamine is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms; further D2 blockade does not help, whereas 5-HT2A antagonism and 5-HT1A or D2 partial agonism increase prefrontal dopamine release.

haloperidol.name: Haloperidol
haloperidol.use: Schizophrenia, acute agitation, delirium (off-label), Tourette syndrome, nausea in palliative care

chlorpromazine.name: Chlorpromazine
chlorpromazine.use: Schizophrenia, mania, intractable hiccups, nausea; the first antipsychotic (1952)

fluphenazine.name: Fluphenazine
fluphenazine.use: Schizophrenia; mainly as the decanoate depot injection

clozapine.name: Clozapine
clozapine.use: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia; suicidal behavior in schizophrenia; Parkinson disease psychosis (low dose)

olanzapine.name: Olanzapine
olanzapine.use: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania and maintenance, acute agitation (IM)

lai.label: pamoate (intramuscular), 405 mg every 4 weeks after 300 mg every 2 weeks for 8 weeks (doses by the oral dose, 150-405 mg every 2-4 weeks); 3-hour observation after each injection
lai.name: Zyprexa Relprevv

quetiapine.name: Quetiapine
quetiapine.use: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania and depression, adjunct in major depression (XR)

ir.name: Seroquel
ir.label: immediate-release tablets, 300 mg twice daily (schizophrenia 300-750 mg/day in divided doses)

xr.name: Seroquel XR
xr.label: extended-release tablets, 600 mg once daily (400-800 mg); peak about 6 hours after the dose

risperidone.name: Risperidone
risperidone.brand: Risperdal, Risperdal Consta, Perseris, Uzedy, Rykindo
risperidone.use: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania, irritability in autism, persistent aggression in dementia (short term)

consta.name: Risperdal Consta
consta.label: microspheres (intramuscular), 25 mg every 2 weeks; main release 3-7 weeks after the injection, oral risperidone for the first 3 weeks

rykindo.name: Rykindo
rykindo.label: microspheres (intramuscular), 25 mg every 2 weeks; initial release, then stable release for 2-4 weeks, oral risperidone for the first week

perseris.name: Perseris
perseris.label: subcutaneous depot, 90 mg monthly; initial release within hours and a second peak at 10-14 days, no oral overlap

uzedy.name: Uzedy
uzedy.label: subcutaneous depot, 75 mg monthly (50-125 mg) or 100-250 mg every 2 months; therapeutic levels within 6-24 hours, no oral overlap

paliperidone.name: Paliperidone
paliperidone.brand: Invega, Invega Sustenna, Invega Trinza, Invega Hafyera, Erzofri
paliperidone.use: Schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder; 1-, 3- and 6-monthly palmitate depots

sustenna.name: Invega Sustenna
sustenna.label: palmitate (intramuscular), 117 mg paliperidone palmitate (75 mg paliperidone) monthly after initiation with 234 mg and 156 mg one week apart

trinza.name: Invega Trinza
trinza.label: palmitate (intramuscular), 410 mg paliperidone palmitate (263 mg paliperidone) every 3 months after at least 4 months of the monthly injection

hafyera.name: Invega Hafyera
hafyera.label: palmitate (intramuscular, gluteal), 1092 mg paliperidone palmitate (700 mg paliperidone) every 6 months after the monthly or 3-monthly injection

erzofri.name: Erzofri
erzofri.label: palmitate (intramuscular), 117 mg paliperidone palmitate (75 mg paliperidone) monthly after a single 351 mg initiation dose

ziprasidone.name: Ziprasidone
ziprasidone.use: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania, acute agitation (IM); take with food (≥ 500 kcal)

lurasidone.name: Lurasidone
lurasidone.use: Schizophrenia, bipolar depression; take with food (≥ 350 kcal)

amisulpride.name: Amisulpride
amisulpride.use: Schizophrenia (high dose); dysthymia (low dose, presynaptic D2/D3 blockade); postoperative nausea (IV, low dose)

aripiprazole.name: Aripiprazole
aripiprazole.brand: Abilify, Abilify Maintena, Abilify Asimtufii, Aristada
aripiprazole.use: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania, adjunct in major depression, irritability in autism, Tourette syndrome

maintena.name: Abilify Maintena
maintena.label: monohydrate (intramuscular), 400 mg monthly (300 mg with adverse effects); oral aripiprazole for 14 days or a 1-day start with two injections

asimtufii.name: Abilify Asimtufii
asimtufii.label: monohydrate (intramuscular), 960 mg every 2 months (720 mg with adverse effects); oral aripiprazole for 14 days or a 1-day start with Abilify Maintena 400 mg

aristada.name: Aristada
aristada.label: lauroxil prodrug (intramuscular), 662 mg aripiprazole lauroxil (≈ 450 mg aripiprazole) monthly; release from day 5-6, started with Aristada Initio 675 mg and 30 mg oral aripiprazole or 21 days of oral aripiprazole

im.name: Abilify
im.label: solution for injection 7.5 mg/mL, 9.75 mg (5.25-15 mg); a second injection after 2 hours if needed, at most 3 injections and 30 mg aripiprazole a day

brexpiprazole.name: Brexpiprazole
brexpiprazole.use: Schizophrenia, adjunct in major depression, agitation in Alzheimer dementia

cariprazine.name: Cariprazine
cariprazine.use: Schizophrenia (incl. predominant negative symptoms), bipolar mania and depression, adjunct in major depression

xanomeline.name: Xanomeline-trospium
xanomeline.use: Schizophrenia in adults (FDA 2024); the first licensed antipsychotic without D2 blockade

pd.label: Xanomeline
pd.note: Xanomeline binds M1-M5 with similar affinity (M4 7 nM) and has its highest agonist activity at M1 and M4. Trospium, a quaternary ammonium antagonist, hardly crosses the blood-brain barrier and blocks peripheral muscarinic receptors.

flupentixol.name: Flupentixol
flupentixol.brand: Fluanxol, Depixol (not marketed in the US)
flupentixol.use: Schizophrenia and other psychoses; at low doses also used for depression with anxiety in some countries

perphenazine.name: Perphenazine
perphenazine.use: Schizophrenia; severe nausea and vomiting in adults

zuclopenthixol.name: Zuclopenthixol
zuclopenthixol.brand: Clopixol, Cisordinol (not marketed in the US)
zuclopenthixol.use: Acute and chronic schizophrenia and other psychoses; mania; the acetate injection for acute agitated psychosis

sertindole.name: Sertindole
sertindole.use: Schizophrenia in patients intolerant of at least one other antipsychotic (QT prolongation; ECG monitoring required)

milsaperidone.name: Milsaperidone
milsaperidone.use: Schizophrenia and acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar I disorder in adults (FDA 2026); interconverts with iloperidone

dopamine.name: Dopamine
dopamine.use: Catecholamine neurotransmitter · salt bridge to Asp114 (3.32), catechol hydroxyls to the TM5 serines

routes.name: Intravenous (IV)
routes.primaryIndications: Delirium and severe agitation in intensive care (haloperidol); postoperative nausea and vomiting (low-dose amisulpride)
routes.advantages: Immediate, titratable effect; little injection-site pain
routes.limitations: QTc prolongation and torsades de pointes (haloperidol) - continuous ECG monitoring advised; not licensed for haloperidol in most countries

routes.name: Intramuscular (IM, short-acting)
routes.primaryIndications: Acute agitation when oral medication is refused (rapid tranquilization)
routes.advantages: Rapid, reliable absorption; higher peak than the same oral dose
routes.limitations: Acute dystonia (haloperidol - often combined with promethazine or a benzodiazepine); hypotension and bradycardia; IM olanzapine must not be combined with parenteral benzodiazepines (cardiorespiratory depression)

routes.name: Orodispersible (ODT)
routes.primaryIndications: Agitation in patients who accept oral medication; suspected non-adherence (cheeking); swallowing difficulty
routes.advantages: Dissolves on the tongue within seconds, so it is hard to hold in the mouth and spit out; no water needed
routes.limitations: Absorption is mostly gastrointestinal, so onset is not faster than the tablet; phenylalanine (aspartame) content

routes.name: Oral (PO)
routes.primaryIndications: Acute and maintenance treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
routes.advantages: Non-invasive; easy dose titration and rapid discontinuation if adverse effects occur
routes.limitations: Partial or non-adherence affects 40-50% of patients and is the main cause of relapse; food effects (ziprasidone, lurasidone require meals)

routes.name: Long-acting injectable (LAI, depot)
routes.commonDrugs: Paliperidone palmitate, aripiprazole, risperidone, olanzapine pamoate, haloperidol and fluphenazine decanoate
routes.primaryIndications: Maintenance treatment of schizophrenia, particularly with non-adherence or a preference for less frequent dosing; first-episode psychosis
routes.advantages: Assured delivery and immediate detection of non-adherence; ≈ 20-30% lower relapse and rehospitalization rates than oral treatment in nationwide cohort studies
routes.limitations: Slow absorption means months to steady state (loading regimens or oral overlap needed) and slow offset of adverse effects; injection-site reactions; post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome with olanzapine pamoate (3-hour observation)

oral.ind: Schizophrenia, mania, delirium, Tourette syndrome
oral.adv: Potent, inexpensive, few metabolic or anticholinergic effects; liquid formulation
oral.caut: High EPS risk (dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia) and tardive dyskinesia; hyperprolactinemia; neuroleptic malignant syndrome

im.adv: Reliable absorption with a higher peak than oral dosing; usually combined with promethazine or lorazepam
im.caut: Acute dystonia (particularly young men) - have an anticholinergic available; ECG recommended before use

iv.ind: Delirium and agitation in intensive care (off-label in most countries)
iv.adv: Titratable; fewer EPS than other routes at equal doses
iv.caut: QTc prolongation and torsades de pointes, dose-related - continuous ECG monitoring; correct potassium and magnesium

lai.ind: Maintenance treatment of schizophrenia with poor adherence
lai.adv: Monthly injection (≈ 10-15× the daily oral dose); long clinical experience and low cost
lai.caut: Apparent t½ ≈ 3 weeks: months to steady state, and EPS resolve slowly after the last injection; oil-based injection is painful

oral.ind: Schizophrenia, mania, intractable hiccups, nausea and vomiting
oral.adv: Marked sedation; broad experience as the original antipsychotic
oral.caut: Orthostatic hypotension, sedation, anticholinergic effects, photosensitivity, cholestatic jaundice, lowered seizure threshold

im.caut: Severe hypotension after IM injection - keep the patient lying down; painful injection

oral.ind: Schizophrenia; oral test dosing before the depot
oral.adv: High potency with little sedation or hypotension
oral.caut: Very low and variable bioavailability; high EPS risk

lai.adv: Every 2-4 weeks; early peak gives a quicker onset than other depots
lai.caut: Early post-injection peak may cause EPS; apparent t½ 7-10 days

oral.onset: 1 h (sedation); antipsychotic effect over weeks to months
oral.ind: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (after two adequate trials); reduction of suicidal behavior
oral.adv: The only antipsychotic with superior efficacy in treatment resistance; lowest EPS and tardive dyskinesia risk
oral.caut: Severe neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count monitoring), myocarditis (first 8 weeks), seizures, constipation and ileus, hypersalivation, orthostatic hypotension (slow titration), metabolic syndrome; levels depend on smoking and CYP1A2 inhibitors

odt.ind: Patients with swallowing difficulty or suspected cheeking

oral.ind: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania and maintenance
oral.adv: Robust efficacy, once-daily dosing, low EPS
oral.caut: Marked weight gain, dyslipidemia and diabetes risk; sedation; levels fall in smokers

odt.ind: Acute agitation in patients who accept oral medication; non-adherence
odt.adv: Dissolves instantly; cannot easily be held in the mouth
odt.caut: Absorption not faster than the tablet

im.adv: Peak concentration ≈ 5× an equal oral dose; fewer EPS than IM haloperidol
im.caut: Do not give with parenteral benzodiazepines (cardiorespiratory depression, deaths reported); hypotension, bradycardia

lai.caut: Post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome (≈ 0.07% of injections): observe for 3 hours in a healthcare facility

oral.ind: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania and depression; adjunct in depression (XR)
oral.adv: Very low EPS and prolactin elevation; preferred in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia when an antipsychotic is unavoidable
oral.caut: Sedation, orthostatic hypotension, weight gain; D2 occupancy is transient (rapid dissociation and short half-life) and high doses are needed for antipsychotic effect

oral.ind: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania, irritability in autism, persistent aggression in Alzheimer dementia (≤ 6 weeks)
oral.adv: Effective at low doses; liquid and orodispersible forms
oral.caut: Dose-dependent EPS above ≈ 6 mg/day; marked hyperprolactinemia (poor blood-brain barrier penetration of the active moiety); orthostatic hypotension on initiation

lai.ind: Maintenance treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder
lai.adv: Microspheres every 2 weeks (Risperdal Consta, Rykindo); subcutaneous depots (Perseris, Uzedy) monthly or every 2 months without a lag or oral overlap
lai.caut: Risperdal Consta releases only after ≈ 3 weeks: continue oral risperidone for the first 3 weeks (Rykindo: 1 week); microspheres need refrigerated storage

oral.ind: Schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder
oral.adv: Once daily, no titration; little hepatic metabolism
oral.caut: Reduce dose in renal impairment; hyperprolactinemia; the OROS shell appears in the stool

lai.ind: Maintenance treatment of schizophrenia; 3- and 6-monthly forms after stabilization
lai.adv: Loading on day 1 and day 8 (deltoid) achieves therapeutic levels within a week without oral overlap; 6-monthly dosing possible
lai.caut: Long apparent half-life (25-49 days, 3-monthly 84-95 days): adverse effects resolve slowly; renal dose adjustment

oral.ind: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania
oral.adv: Weight- and lipid-neutral
oral.caut: Must be taken with a meal (≥ 500 kcal) or absorption halves; QTc prolongation (≈ 10 ms); avoid other QT-prolonging drugs

im.adv: Low EPS compared with IM haloperidol

oral.ind: Schizophrenia (adults and adolescents), bipolar depression
oral.adv: Low metabolic and QTc liability; antidepressant efficacy in bipolar depression
oral.caut: Take with ≥ 350 kcal; contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers; akathisia and somnolence

oral.ind: Schizophrenia (400-800 mg/day); dysthymia (50 mg/day)
oral.adv: No hepatic metabolism, few interactions; minimal sedation and weight gain
oral.caut: Highest prolactin elevation of all antipsychotics; QTc prolongation; accumulates in renal impairment

iv.ind: Prevention and treatment of postoperative nausea and vomiting (5-10 mg)
iv.adv: Low dose acts at D2/D3 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, outside the blood-brain barrier

oral.ind: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania, adjunct in major depression, irritability in autism, Tourette syndrome
oral.adv: Low metabolic risk; lowers prolactin (used to treat antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia); little sedation
oral.caut: Akathisia, restlessness, insomnia, nausea; impulse-control disorders (gambling); halve the dose in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers

lai.onset: Days (oral overlap 14 days, or two-injection start)
lai.ind: Maintenance treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder
lai.adv: Monthly or 2-monthly injection with the low metabolic risk of aripiprazole
lai.caut: Oral overlap for 14 days (or a two-injection start) is needed; dose reduction with CYP2D6 or 3A4 inhibitors

im.ind: Rapid control of agitation in schizophrenia or mania when oral treatment is not appropriate
im.adv: Absolute bioavailability 100 % and faster early exposure than tablets; little sedation, EPS or QTc effect
im.caut: Orthostatic hypotension; less calming than haloperidol or olanzapine injection; switch to oral treatment as soon as possible

oral.ind: Schizophrenia, adjunct in major depression, agitation in Alzheimer dementia
oral.adv: Lower intrinsic activity than aripiprazole: less akathisia and insomnia
oral.caut: Weight gain (modest); dose reduction with CYP2D6 or 3A4 inhibitors; increased mortality in older adults with dementia (boxed warning)

oral.ind: Schizophrenia including predominant negative symptoms, bipolar mania and depression, adjunct in depression
oral.adv: D3-preferring partial agonist; low metabolic and prolactin effects
oral.caut: Akathisia; very long-lived active metabolite (didesmethylcariprazine): dose changes take weeks to reach steady state

metabolism.name: Risperidone → paliperidone (9-hydroxyrisperidone)
metabolism.note: The metabolite is as active as the parent, so the "active moiety" (risperidone + 9-OH-risperidone) determines the effect. In CYP2D6 normal (extensive) metabolizers risperidone is converted quickly (t½ ≈ 3 h) and 9-OH-risperidone predominates; in poor metabolizers (about 7 % of Europeans) risperidone has a t½ of about 20 h and the parent predominates, but the active moiety and the clinical effect are similar. Paliperidone is mostly excreted unchanged, so the dose is reduced in renal impairment.

metabolism.name: Clozapine: CYP1A2-dependent demethylation
metabolism.note: CYP1A2 dominates, so smoking (induction) lowers and fluvoxamine (inhibition) or stopping smoking raises clozapine levels several-fold; the clozapine/norclozapine ratio (normally ≈ 1.3-2) helps interpret levels. Inflammation and infection suppress CYP1A2 and can cause toxicity.

metabolism.name: Aripiprazole → dehydroaripiprazole
metabolism.note: Dehydroaripiprazole has D2 affinity similar to the parent and reaches ≈ 40% of its exposure at steady state. Both are cleared by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4: halve the dose in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers or with strong 2D6 or 3A4 inhibitors, quarter it with both.

metabolism.name: Cariprazine: two sequential active metabolites
metabolism.note: Didesmethylcariprazine (t½ 1-3 weeks) dominates at steady state, so effects and adverse effects (e.g. akathisia) may appear weeks after a dose change and persist for weeks after stopping.

metabolism.name: Olanzapine: direct glucuronidation and CYP1A2
metabolism.note: No active metabolites. Clearance is ≈ 40% higher in smokers and ≈ 30% lower in women and older adults, which together explain much of the variability in levels.

cyp2d6_pm.label: CYP2D6 poor metabolizer

cyp3a4_inh.label: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor

tha.activation: Gating of sensory information relayed to the cortex

hyp.activation: Tuberoinfundibular dopamine neurons inhibit prolactin release
hyp.blockade: Prolactin elevation together with blockade at the pituitary
hyp.pathway: Tuberoinfundibular: origin in the arcuate nucleus; blockade raises prolactin

hip.pathway: Mesolimbic: target of VTA dopamine neurons; overactivity is linked to positive symptoms

bs.note: Substantia nigra and VTA: somatodendritic autoreceptors
bs.activation: Somatodendritic autoreceptors slow the firing of dopamine neurons (substantia nigra, VTA)
bs.blockade: Autoreceptor blockade increases dopamine release, mainly at low doses
bs.pathway: Origin of the mesolimbic and mesocortical (VTA) and nigrostriatal (substantia nigra) pathways

pit.pathway: Tuberoinfundibular: target of the pathway; blockade raises prolactin

ctx.activation: Inhibitory control of prefrontal cognitive function
ctx.pathway: Mesocortical: D3 blockade is proposed to improve cognitive symptoms

ob.activation: Reward processing in the islands of Calleja

str.note: Ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens shell) rather than dorsal

str.blockade: Possible effect on negative symptoms (proposed for cariprazine)
str.pathway: Mesolimbic: D3 is concentrated in the accumbens shell; D3 blockade is proposed to ease negative symptoms

bs.pathway: Autoreceptors on VTA and substantia nigra neurons regulate all three midbrain pathways

ctx.note: Prefrontal and cingulate cortex, layers I-II and V
ctx.activation: Increases prefrontal dopamine release; mood and cognition (partial agonists such as aripiprazole)
ctx.pathway: Mesocortical: agonism increases prefrontal dopamine, possibly easing negative and cognitive symptoms

hyp.activation: Cortisol release and lower body temperature

hip.activation: Anxiolytic and antidepressant effects (as with buspirone)

bs.activation: Raphe autoreceptors reduce the firing of serotonin neurons
bs.pathway: Raphe serotonin neurons modulate dopamine neurons in the VTA and substantia nigra

sc.activation: Pain modulation in the dorsal horn

ctx.note: Neocortex layer V pyramidal neurons; claustrum
ctx.activation: Hallucinations and altered perception (psychedelics act here)
ctx.blockade: Antihallucinatory effect (pimavanserin) and deeper slow-wave sleep
ctx.pathway: Mesocortical: blockade increases prefrontal dopamine, possibly easing negative and cognitive symptoms

ctx.blockade: Possible antidepressant effect through more prefrontal dopamine and norepinephrine
ctx.pathway: Mesocortical: blockade increases prefrontal dopamine; possible benefit for negative symptoms and mood

str.pathway: Mesolimbic: 5-HT2C tonically inhibits dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens

hyp.note: Arcuate nucleus POMC neurons (appetite); choroid plexus has the highest density of all

hyp.blockade: Increased appetite and weight gain, together with H1 blockade (olanzapine, clozapine)

bs.activation: Inhibits dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra and VTA
bs.pathway: Mesolimbic and mesocortical: 5-HT2C on VTA GABA interneurons inhibits dopamine neurons

hyp.note: Tuberomammillary nucleus and its local targets
hyp.blockade: Increased appetite and weight gain (clozapine, olanzapine)

ctx.activation: Attention and memory; M1/M4 agonism by xanomeline is thought to contribute to its antipsychotic effect

ctx.pathway: M1 agonism (xanomeline) is proposed to improve cognitive symptoms
